warmup.q: interface Dispenser<T> { fun next(): T } and fun total(d: Dispenser<Fruit>). You have a Dispenser<Apple>. What do you need for total(apples) to compile?
options: Nothing: Apple is a Fruit, so it already compiles
Declare interface Dispenser<out T>, because a dispenser only hands T out
Cast: total(apples as Dispenser<Fruit>) is the normal way
warmup.why: Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise, so the call doesn't compile yet. Dispenser only produces T, so a dispenser of apples can safely act as a dispenser of fruit. out tells the compiler that. in is for the opposite case, consumers, which lesson 5 of this track covers.

opening:
By the shop door stands an apple dispenser. Pull the lever, and an apple drops out. A customer who wants "some fruit" can use it happily, because every apple that drops out is a fruit. There's no slot to put anything in, and that's the whole point.

In code, the compiler doesn't know that your class has no slot. A Dispenser<Apple> won't pass as a Dispenser<Fruit> until you tell it, and you tell it with one small word on the declaration. That word is easy to misread as "read-only" or "immutable". It's neither.

Lesson 3 of this track ended with a read-only List<String> passing as a List<Any>, because the standard library declares List<out E>. In this lesson, we'll write that out ourselves on a dispenser, and learn where T may appear once we do. Then we'll line up Kotlin's List with Java's ? extends, and empty a dispenser to see what out doesn't promise. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the shop door, with a dispenser that has a lever and no slot. out T writes that down: T only comes out, so a Dispenser<Apple> can stand in for a Dispenser<Fruit>, and the compiler checks every member for a hidden slot. It still doesn't stop anyone from emptying the dispenser.

Now look in your own code for a generic class whose type parameter appears only in return types and vals, such as a result holder. If it isn't declared out, its callers pay with copies and casts.

Next, we'll turn the dispenser around: a bin you only drop things into. If an apple dispenser is a fruit dispenser, which way does the arrow point for a bin?

sections.h: A dispenser only hands values out: covariance with out
sections.html:
A producer is a type whose values of T only ever come out of it. The apple dispenser is one. So are an iterator, a page of search results, and a Java Supplier, the JDK interface whose get() hands you a value. You call it, and it hands you a T. Nothing about it takes a T in.

Here is the dispenser in code. next() hands out the next item, or null when the dispenser is empty. The shop's fruit are the same as before: a Fruit interface with a name and a weight, and Apple and Lemon as data classes that implement it. gala and fuji below are two apples, of 180 g and 150 g.

Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track on the dispenser: ask whether a secret swap could make any allowed call go wrong. Suppose some code expects a dispenser of Fruit, and you hand it a dispenser of Apple. Every call it can make returns an Apple, and every Apple is a Fruit. Nothing can go wrong. So it's safe to treat a Dispenser<Apple> as a Dispenser<Fruit>.

The compiler can't see that by itself. Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise: a Dispenser<Apple> and a Dispenser<Fruit> are simply unrelated types. In Kotlin, you say otherwise on the declaration, once, with out. Java has no such keyword, so it says it at every use, with the wildcard ? extends, Java's way of writing "some subtype of":

Java
interface Dispenser<T> {
    T next();                                       // null when it is empty
}

static int totalGrams(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { ... }

Dispenser<Apple> apples = listDispenser(List.of(gala, fuji));
totalGrams(apples);                                 // fine: the parameter says ? extends
Dispenser<Fruit> plain = apples;                    // error: Dispenser<Apple> cannot be converted to Dispenser<Fruit>
Kotlin
interface Dispenser<out T> {
    fun next(): T?                                  // null when it is empty
}

fun totalGrams(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>): Int { ... }

val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = ListDispenser(listOf(gala, fuji))
totalGrams(apples)                                  // fine: Dispenser is declared out
val plain: Dispenser<Fruit> = apples                // also fine

ProducerDemo in the labs runs both versions, and both print apple total: 330 g. Remove the out, and Kotlin behaves like Java's plain Dispenser<T>:

error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Dispenser<Apple>', but 'Dispenser<Fruit>' was expected.

This property is called covariance: the subtype arrow between the element types carries over, in the same direction, to the generic type. Apple is a subtype of Fruit, so Dispenser<Apple> is a subtype of Dispenser<Fruit>. The figure shows the two arrows side by side. In short, an apple dispenser is a fruit dispenser, because only apples come out.

Where you write out matters. Kotlin's out on the declaration is called declaration-site variance: you think about it once, when you write Dispenser, and every user gets the flexible behavior for free. Java's ? extends is use-site variance: every method that takes a dispenser must remember to write it, and the ones that forget are stricter than they need to be. Lesson 6 of this track shows that Kotlin has the use-site form too, for types that can't be out everywhere.

A type that only hands T out can stand in for a dispenser of any supertype. Say so with out.

That raises the obvious question: what stops someone from adding a slot?

try.title: Take out away and watch the call break
steps: Run ProducerDemo (or ProducerDemoJava) with the command below. Both print the same total.
In ProducerDemo.kt, remove out from both interface Dispenser<out T> and class ListDispenser<out T>. Predict which line fails, then run.
Put out back. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. Why does Java need ? extends on totalGrams, while Kotlin needs nothing there?

code.title: ProducerDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo // The shop's fruit, used by every demo of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit /** A producer: T only comes out. `out` tells the compiler so. */ interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T? // null when it is empty } class ListDispenser<out T>(items: List<T>) : Dispenser<T> { private val it = items.iterator() override fun next(): T? = if (it.hasNext()) it.next() else null } /** Needs a Dispenser<Fruit>. Because Dispenser is `out`, a Dispenser<Apple> fits. */ fun totalGrams(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>): Int { var sum = 0 while (true) { val fruit = dispenser.next() ?: break sum += fruit.grams } return sum } fun main() { val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = ListDispenser(listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))) println("apple total: ${totalGrams(apples)} g") // a Dispenser<Apple> used as a Dispenser<Fruit> val anything: Dispenser<Any> = ListDispenser(listOf("a paper bag")) // Dispenser<String> used as Dispenser<Any> println("first from anything: ${anything.next()}") }

alt.title: ProducerDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ProducerDemo.kt. Java has no `out` on a declaration, so Dispenser<T> stays invariant * and every method that wants "a dispenser of some kind of Fruit" says so at the use site: ? extends. * Fruit and Apple are the Kotlin types from ProducerDemo.kt. */ public class ProducerDemoJava { interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); // null when it is empty } static <T> Dispenser<T> listDispenser(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // ? extends Fruit: "a Dispenser of Fruit or of some subtype". Without it, a Dispenser<Apple> would not fit. static int totalGrams(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { int sum = 0; for (Fruit f = dispenser.next(); f != null; f = dispenser.next()) sum += f.getGrams(); return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { Dispenser<Apple> apples = listDispenser(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); System.out.println("apple total: " + totalGrams(apples) + " g"); Dispenser<? extends Object> anything = listDispenser(List.of("a paper bag")); System.out.println("first from anything: " + anything.next()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Dispenser<Fruit> plain = apples; } }

try.expect: Both versions print apple total: 330 g and first from anything: a paper bag. Without out, Kotlin fails on totalGrams(apples) with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Dispenser<Apple>', but 'Dispenser<Fruit>' was expected. The Dispenser<Any> line still compiles, because Kotlin infers T = Any for that new dispenser. The Java wrong move fails with incompatible types: Dispenser<Apple> cannot be converted to Dispenser<Fruit>. Java's Dispenser<T> is invariant, so each method that wants flexibility writes ? extends. Kotlin wrote out once, on the interface.

sections.h: Where T may appear: in, out and invariant positions
sections.html:
A Dispenser<out T> can't also have a fun refill(item: T), and the substitution test shows why. out lets you pass apples, a Dispenser<Apple>, where a Dispenser<Fruit> is expected. Through that view, refill(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) type-checks, because a lemon is a Fruit. Now a dispenser that hands out apples holds a lemon, and the next next() gives it to code that reads it as an Apple: a ClassCastException, far from the refill. An apple dispenser with a slot for any fruit stops being an apple dispenser. It becomes a surprise machine.

The compiler can't allow both things: treating a Dispenser<Apple> as a Dispenser<Fruit>, and a parameter of type T. With out, it keeps the first and rejects the parameter.

out is a promise: "values of T only come out of this type". The compiler holds you to it by checking every member that outside code can call for a hidden slot. Each place where T appears has a position:

  • A return type is an out-position. The value flows out to the caller.
  • A parameter type is an in-position. The value flows in from the caller.
  • A var property is both at once, because it has a getter and a setter. That is an invariant position.

In a class declared out T, T may appear only in out-positions. Try to break the rule, and the error names the position:

Java
// Java has no `out` on the declaration, so it checks the same rule where you USE the type:
interface Producer<T> {
    T produce();
    void consume(T item);
}

Producer<? extends Object> view = strings;   // strings is a Producer<String>
Object out = view.produce();     // fine: T comes out
view.consume("Fuji");            // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1
Kotlin
interface Producer<out T> {
    fun produce(): T             // fine
    val latest: T                // fine: a val only has a getter
    fun consume(item: T)         // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position
    var current: T               // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position
}

The full Kotlin message reads type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of interface Producer<out T>)'. Java's CAP#1 is javac's name for "the unknown subtype behind ? extends". Java can't promise that any String fits it, so it refuses the call.

Three special cases come up all the time in Kotlin.

First, constructor parameters are fine, as long as they are plain parameters or val properties. class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T) compiles. Building the object puts a T in, but only once, while the real type is still known. A var constructor property is a var, so class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) fails with the invariant-position error.

Second, private members are exempt. private var hidden: T and private fun replace(t: T) are allowed, because no outside code can call them with the wrong type. protected and internal members are checked like public ones.

Third, private set is not enough. var lastServed: T? = null with private set still fails, with occurs in 'invariant' position, because the property is still a var. The fix is to split it into a private var for the class and a public val that reads it. The lab makes you do exactly that.

These rules can feel strict on a dispenser you wrote yourself. They feel obvious on a type you have used for years.

try.title: Find the positions the compiler rejects
steps: Open PositionsDemo.kt. For the four numbered lines, predict the position the error will name: in or invariant.
Uncomment each line on its own and run. Comment it out again before the next.
Run PositionsDemoJava and uncomment its view.consume line. Where does Java report the same rule?

code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** Which members may mention T in a class declared `out T`? Uncomment ONE line at a time and run. */ interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // return type: out-position, fine val latest: T // val: out-position, fine // fun consume(item: T) // 1 // var current: T // 2 } class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T, private var hidden: T) { // all three are fine private fun replace(t: T) { hidden = t } // private: exempt fun first(): T = item // protected fun keep(t: T) {} // 3 } // class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) // 4 fun main() { val h: Holder<Any> = Holder("Gala", "x", "y") println("Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: ${h.first()}") }

alt.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo; /** * Java twin of PositionsDemo.kt. Java cannot mark a declaration `out`, so the same rule shows up * where you USE the type: through a `? extends` reference you may call methods that return T, * and javac refuses calls that pass a T in. */ public class PositionsDemoJava { interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); // allowed in the declaration: Java checks the use site } public static void main(String[] args) { Producer<String> strings = new Producer<>() { String last = "Gala"; public String produce() { return last; } public void consume(String item) { last = item; } }; Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; // the Java spelling of "used as Producer<out Any>" Object out = view.produce(); // fine: out-position System.out.println("produced " + out); // Wrong move. The demo itself prints Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: Gala. Java reports the rule at the call: String cannot be converted to CAP#1, because Java checks variance where you use a type, not where you declare it.

sections.h: List<out E> is the dispenser you already use, and Java's ? extends
sections.html:
You have used a covariant type every day: Kotlin's read-only List. Its declaration is public interface List<out E> : Collection<E>. That out is why a List<Apple> goes into any function that takes a List<Fruit>, with no ceremony at all:

Java
static int totalWeight(List<? extends Fruit> fruit) {     // the wildcard is the flexible part
    int sum = 0;
    for (Fruit f : fruit) sum += f.getGrams();
    return sum;
}

static int totalWeightInvariant(List<Fruit> fruit) { ... }

List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji));
totalWeight(apples);              // fine
totalWeightInvariant(apples);     // error: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>
Kotlin
fun totalWeight(fruit: List<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams }

fun totalWeightMutable(fruit: MutableList<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams }

val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(gala, fuji)
totalWeight(apples)               // fine: List is out
totalWeightMutable(apples)        // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', but 'MutableList<Fruit>' was expected

The two snippets line up exactly. Java's List<? extends Fruit> and Kotlin's List<Fruit> are the same contract: "a list I will only read from, of Fruit or any subtype". Java's plain List<Fruit> and Kotlin's MutableList<Fruit> are the strict, invariant version.

Kotlin keeps this promise when Java code calls it. When a parameter's type is declared out, Kotlin writes a ? extends into the Java signature. javap, the JDK tool that prints what a class file contains, shows it for ListOutDemo:

public static final int totalWeight(java.util.List<? extends workbench.generics.l04.demo.Fruit>);
public static final int totalWeightMutable(java.util.List<workbench.generics.l04.demo.Fruit>);

So Java callers can pass a List<Apple> to totalWeight too. The demo's Java twin does exactly that, and prints Kotlin's totalWeight(apples) from Java = 330. Kotlin leaves the wildcard out in two places. One is return types, so Java callers don't have to handle wildcards. The other is a final type argument, a class like String that nothing can extend, where ? extends String would mean nothing. The lab's tests use this rule to check your out: they read the Java signature of your function and look for ? extends.

So out is cheap, checked by the compiler, and visible from Java. What it isn't is a lock.

sections.h: out does not mean immutable: the dispenser can still be emptied
sections.html:
The most common wrong idea about covariance is that out means read-only, or immutable. It doesn't. out only limits which types can flow in. State can still change.

Here the dispenser picture breaks, in a useful way. A real dispenser has no slot for customers, but the shop assistant can still open it, empty it or refill it. out says nothing about any of that.

Shelf below keeps its items in a private MutableList<T>, which is allowed, because private members are exempt. take() removes an item and still only hands a T out, the way an assistant can eat the last apple without ever using the slot. clear() mentions no T at all. Both are legal in an out class. Java's ? extends view behaves the same way, and so does Kotlin's MutableList<out Fruit>, the same idea written where the type is used (lesson 6 of this track covers it):

Java
List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji));
List<? extends Fruit> view = apples;       // "read-only" for the type only

Fruit taken = view.remove(0);              // fine: remove hands a value out
view.clear();                              // fine: no T involved
view.add(new Apple("Pink Lady", 170));     // error: Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1
Kotlin
class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) {
    fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0)      // changes state, only hands T out
    fun clear() = items.clear()            // changes state, no T at all
}

val view: MutableList<out Fruit> = mutableListOf(Apple("Braeburn", 200))
view.removeAt(0)                           // fine
view.clear()                               // fine
view.add(Apple("Pink Lady", 170))          // error: contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E)'

ImmutableMythDemo prints took Gala, 1 left, then after clear: 0 left. The MutableList<out Fruit> view loses its only apple too: view after removeAt: 0 left. Only the add is refused. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: the only thing variance guarantees is type safety, and immutability is a different story.

So when you need a class to be covariant, but it also seems to need a method that takes a T, you have three honest options:

  1. Move the method out of the class as an extension function, a function declared outside the class that you call as if it were a member. fun <T> Dispenser<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T declares its own T, so the class's variance rules don't apply. The standard library does this: plus(element: T) and getOrElse on List are extensions.
  2. Give the method its own type parameter, such as fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Tray<R>. Here T sits inside the parameter of a function parameter, and two in-positions cancel out. Lesson 5 of this track shows why.
  3. Split the type in two: a covariant read interface and an invariant read-write one, like List and MutableList.

There is also @UnsafeVariance, which switches the check off for one position. List.contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E) uses it, because contains only compares. It's a promise you make by hand, and lesson 10 of this track shows how to break it.

That is also where out stops. It only fits a type whose T never goes in. Some types are the exact opposite: a bin you only drop things into never hands a T back. For those, out is the wrong promise, and the next lesson writes the other one.

try.title: Empty a covariant shelf
steps: Run ImmutableMythDemo (or ImmutableMythDemoJava). Before it runs, predict whether take() and clear() compile in a class declared out T.
Uncomment the view.add line and run. Read which rule stops it.

code.title: ImmutableMythDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** `out` limits which TYPES flow in. It does not stop state from changing. */ class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { // a private MutableList<T> is fine in an out class fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, still only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, mentions no T at all val size: Int get() = items.size } fun main() { val shelf: Shelf<Fruit> = Shelf(mutableListOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))) println("took ${shelf.take().name}, ${shelf.size} left") shelf.clear() println("after clear: ${shelf.size} left") // The same is true of a use-site out projection: no add, but clear and removeAt still work. val view: MutableList<out Fruit> = mutableListOf(Apple("Braeburn", 200)) view.removeAt(0) println("view after removeAt: ${view.size} left") // view.add(Apple("Pink Lady", 170)) // uncomment: which rule stops this? }

alt.title: ImmutableMythDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ImmutableMythDemo.kt. A ? extends view stops adds, not changes. Fruit and Apple come from ProducerDemo.kt. */ public class ImmutableMythDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; // read-only for the TYPE, not for the state Fruit taken = view.remove(0); // compiles: remove hands a value out System.out.println("took " + taken.getName() + ", " + view.size() + " left"); view.clear(); // compiles: no T involved System.out.println("after clear: " + view.size() + " left, and apples has " + apples.size()); // view.add(new Apple("Pink Lady", 170)); // uncomment: which rule stops this? } }

try.expect: It prints took Gala, 1 left, after clear: 0 left and, in Kotlin, view after removeAt: 0 left. Variance never stopped the state from changing. The add fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. in Kotlin, and with Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1 in Java: only the in-position is blocked.

compare.title: A producer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java

java.title: Dispensers.java
java.html: import java.util.List; interface Fruit { int grams(); } record Apple(int grams) implements Fruit {} // Java can't say "T only comes out" on the declaration interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); } class Dispensers { // every method that should accept subtypes must remember ? extends static int total(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser, int n) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += dispenser.next().grams(); return sum; } static int sum(List<? extends Fruit> fruit) { return fruit.stream().mapToInt(Fruit::grams).sum(); } // forget it once, and the method is stricter than it needs to be static int strict(Dispenser<Fruit> dispenser) { return dispenser.next().grams(); } }

kotlin.title: Dispensers.kt
kotlin.html: interface Fruit { val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val grams: Int) : Fruit // say it once, on the declaration interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T } // plain types in every signature: Dispenser and List are both covariant fun total(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>, n: Int): Int { var sum = 0 repeat(n) { sum += dispenser.next().grams } return sum } fun sum(fruit: List<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams } // the compiler enforces the promise inside Dispenser: // fun refill(t: T) would fail with "declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position"

compare.note: The safety rule is the same in both languages: through a covariant view you may take values out, but not put them in. The difference is who carries the burden. In Java, the type stays invariant, and every method signature has to say ? extends, so the flexibility depends on each author remembering. In Kotlin, the author of Dispenser says out once, the compiler checks every member of Dispenser against it, and every signature that mentions Dispenser<Fruit> is flexible without extra work. When Java calls that Kotlin code, Kotlin writes the ? extends into the parameter types for it.

worked.title: Make the shop's Dispenser covariant without losing a feature

steps.say: The shop's weighing report takes a Dispenser<Fruit>, but the apple dispenser is a Dispenser<Apple>. The dispenser only hands items out, so it should be covariant. Here it is before the change. lastServed remembers the last item handed out, and nextOr gives a fallback when the dispenser is empty.
steps.code: class Dispenser<T>(items: List<T>) { private val queue = ArrayDeque(items) var lastServed: T? = null private set fun hasNext(): Boolean = queue.isNotEmpty() fun next(): T { val item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item } fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (queue.isEmpty()) fallback else next() }

alt.html: class Dispenser<T> { private final ArrayDeque<T> queue; private T lastServed; Dispenser(List<T> items) { queue = new ArrayDeque<>(items); } boolean hasNext() { return !queue.isEmpty(); } T next() { T item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item; } T nextOr(T fallback) { return queue.isEmpty() ? fallback : next(); } T lastServed() { return lastServed; } }

steps.say: 1. Add out and read the errors. The compiler names two members. nextOr takes a T, an in-position. lastServed is a var, so its type is in an invariant position, even with a private setter. In Java there is nothing to add to the class; each caller writes Dispenser<? extends Fruit> instead.
steps.code: class Dispenser<out T>(items: List<T>) { // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'T?' var lastServed: T? = null private set // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T' fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = ... }

alt.html: // Java checks at the use site instead: static List<Fruit> drainAll(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { ... } Dispenser<? extends Fruit> view = appleDispenser; Fruit f = view.next(); // fine view.nextOr(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); // error: cannot be converted to CAP#1

steps.say: 1. Fix the property by splitting it: a private var (exempt) and a public val (an out-position). Callers still read lastServed, and nobody outside could set it before either.
steps.code: private var last: T? = null val lastServed: T? get() = last

alt.html: private T last; T lastServed() { return last; } // Java: a getter with no setter

steps.say: 1. Fix nextOr by moving it out of the class as an extension. The extension declares its own T, so the class's out doesn't constrain it. Self-check: why is this safe? (At the call apples.nextOr(x), the compiler picks a T that fits both the dispenser and x. For a Dispenser<Apple> and a Lemon fallback, that T is Fruit, and the result is typed Fruit.)
steps.code: fun <T> Dispenser<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (hasNext()) next() else fallback val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = Dispenser(listOf(Apple("Gala", 180))) val f: Fruit = apples.nextOr(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // T = Fruit

alt.html: // Java: a static helper with its own <T> does the same job static <T> T nextOr(Dispenser<? extends T> dispenser, T fallback) { return dispenser.hasNext() ? dispenser.next() : fallback; } Fruit f = nextOr(appleDispenser, new Lemon("Eureka", 120));

lab.title: Make Dispenser and Tray covariant
steps: Read Fruit.kt: the same Fruit, Apple and Lemon as in this lesson. Then run the tests. Eight of nine fail. Read the two variance failures, which say expected: "Dispenser<? extends Fruit>" (and the same for Tray) but was: "Dispenser<Fruit>". The test reads the Java signature of drainAll, which only gets a wildcard when Dispenser is declared out.
In Dispenser.kt, add out to Dispenser's type parameter. Run the tests, and read the compile error about lastServed.
Fix lastServed without making it settable from outside: split it into a private var and a public val with a getter.
Tray.kt holds a tray of items with a label card, like the fruit in the shop window. Add out to Tray. Predict whether map still compiles before you run. Then write map and firstOnTray.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: private var last: T? = null plus val lastServed: T? get() = last keeps the read for callers and the write for the class.
ArrayDeque.removeFirst() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty deque, which is what next() should do.
map compiles under out: in f: (T) -> R, T is the parameter of a parameter, which counts as an out-position. Tray(items.map(f), label) is the whole body.

drill.title: Write a producer from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a covariant Dispenser interface with one method next(), a ListDispenser class that implements it over a List, and a function totalGrams that accepts a dispenser of apples as a dispenser of fruit. Write it in Kotlin with out, then in Java with ? extends. Then add a refill(t: T) member to the Kotlin interface, and write down the error you expect.

answer.html: interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T? } class ListDispenser<out T>(items: List<T>) : Dispenser<T> { private val it = items.iterator() override fun next(): T? = if (it.hasNext()) it.next() else null } fun totalGrams(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>): Int { var sum = 0 while (true) sum += (dispenser.next() ?: break).grams return sum } // fun refill(t: T) inside Dispenser: // error: type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position

alt.title: Dispenser.java
alt.html: interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); // null when it is empty } static <T> Dispenser<T> listDispenser(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // the flexibility lives in the parameter, not in Dispenser static int totalGrams(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { int sum = 0; for (Fruit f = dispenser.next(); f != null; f = dispenser.next()) sum += f.grams(); return sum; }

recap: A producer only hands values of T out. A producer of a subtype can safely stand in for a producer of the supertype, the way an apple dispenser is a fruit dispenser: that is covariance.
Kotlin declares it once, with out T on the declaration. Java writes ? extends T at every use.
In an out class, T may appear in return types and vals, not in parameters or vars. Constructor vals and private members are fine; private set is not enough.

Kotlin's read-only List<out E> is why a List<Apple> fits a List<Fruit> parameter, and Kotlin writes ? extends into Java parameter signatures for out types (except for final type arguments and return types).
The limit: out controls which types flow in, not whether state changes, and it only fits types whose T never goes in. A type that only takes T in needs the opposite promise.

explain.prompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate why Kotlin lets a Tray<Apple> be passed where a Tray<Fruit> is expected once Tray is declared out T, and what the compiler asks of Tray in return.
explain.answer: Tray only hands items out: you read items and map them, and nothing in its public members takes a T in. If I give you a tray of apples where you expected a tray of fruit, every item you read really is a fruit, so nothing can go wrong. out T is my promise that this is true, and in return the compiler lets the subtype arrow carry over from Apple to Tray<Apple>. To keep the promise honest, the compiler rejects any public member where T would flow in, like a parameter of type T or a var: there must be no slot. In Java, the same idea is written at each use as Tray<? extends Fruit>.

deeper.html:
The rule "parameters are in-positions" has a twist when the parameter is itself a function. In fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R), T is the input of f. The tray calls f and passes it a T, so the value flows out of the tray into the caller's lambda. Two in-positions cancel out. That is why map is legal in Tray<out T>, while fun replay(): (T) -> Unit (a function returned to the caller, which the caller will feed a T) is not. Lesson 5 of this track turns this into a sign rule.

Kotlin is strict about inferred types too. In class E<in T> { private fun produce(): T? = null; fun use() = produce() }, the private produce is fine, but the public use() has the inferred return type T?, and fails. Give public members of variant classes explicit types.

Private members get one more rule, called private-to-this. Inside class C<out T>(private var t: T), the method fun copyFrom(o: C<@UnsafeVariance T>) { t = o.t } fails with cannot access 'var t: T': it is private/*private to this*/. A private member is only exempt when you reach it through this, because another instance o might really be a C<Subtype> seen as a C<T>.

Finally, Kotlin leaves the wildcard out of Java signatures when the type argument is final. fun f(x: List<String>) is f(List<String>) in Java, because nothing can extend String. Use @JvmWildcard to force one, or @JvmSuppressWildcards to drop them.
